facts.raw_span: 1 day of chest pressure
subjective fevers, rhinorrhea, a dry cough, and sinus congestion
3 hours of substernal pressure that resolved spontaneously
constant chest pressure radiating to the right jaw, diaphoresis, and 1 episode of vomiting
Vital signs obtained in the Emergency Department were within normal limits
Cardiac examination revealed a regular rate and rhythm, normal point of maximum impulse without lifts, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops in supine, sitting, or standing positions
Initial serum troponin I level: 6.18 ng/mL
Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein
Normal sinus rhythm, ST-segment elevations with PR-segment depression in leads II, III, and aVF, ST-segment depression in lead V1, and PR-segment elevation in lead aVR
Normal coronary arteries, left ventricular end-diastolic pressure 12 mm Hg
Normal results
No medical history

concepts.why: The patient presented with chest pressure and had an elevated serum troponin I level, which is a key indicator of acute coronary syndrome.
The patient had elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, and ST-segment elevations with PR-segment depression, which are consistent with myopericarditis.
The patient had ST-segment elevations with PR-segment depression, which is a characteristic electrocardiographic finding in acute pericarditis.

The patient had a recent history of subjective fevers, rhinorrhea, a dry cough, and sinus congestion, which may be indicative of a viral infection, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, which are consistent with viral pericarditis.

rationales.F01: Chest pressure is a common symptom of acute coronary syndrome and pericarditis.
rationales.F07: Elevated troponin levels are indicative of myocardial injury, which can be seen in acute coronary syndrome, myopericarditis, and pericarditis.
rationales.F09: ST-segment elevations with PR-segment depression are characteristic of acute pericarditis.
rationales.F10: Normal coronary arteries make acute coronary syndrome less likely.

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient's presentation with chest pressure, ST-segment elevations, and PR-segment depression in leads II, III, and aVF, along with normal coronary arteries and elevated inflammatory markers, is most consistent with Acute Pericarditis. The absence of significant cardiac examination abnormalities and the presence of viral prodrome symptoms also support this diagnosis.
